utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Again, our excuses for a late start. We had a discussion in the Chamber which was not finalised. I would like to ask the Defence what is the position in relation to two exhibits I raised that two days ago? And Mr. Gajic promised us at the latest, yesterday, at the beginning of the hearing to make a response. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since P13165 [as interpreted] and P13163 have been translated, 3163 actually is a photograph, so we could lift the MFI status and have them admitted as proper exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But the number was translated incorrectly. The P numbers are P1362 and P1363. They both will be now admitted and no longer MFI'd. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, now it's your turn with the re-examination, if there are no other matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, Mr. Manning is ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I wanted to show that document which apparently was not uploaded into e-court, so we'll need, it's D169, to turn on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And again under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Manning. Please sit down. I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey is commencing his re-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, I just want to touch on this document again, we'll try to wait a bit until we actually -- it'll come up -- should come up on the ELMO. But this is the -- just to remind everyone, the letter that was discussed yesterday to Mr. Masovic, the Bosnian commission on missing persons. And as you recall, you mentioned remembering a letter in your direct testimony so we went and looked and I just wanted to know, do you know if this was the letter that you were thinking of? As you know, there's many letters in these -- on these topics, and if you need to take a moment to look at it, please do.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I believe that's the document I was referring to which indicated we were handing over responsibility for those graves, which I note are also attached at the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I just want to call your attention to a line in the last paragraph, and since we don't have a translation, I'll read that slowly. It's the third paragraph on the first page, the last line, and it says: "In order to expedite the exhumation process, the OTP now seeks the assistance of the appropriate authorities (Commissions) in conducting the remaining exhumations of the secondary gravesites." Do you recall what we mean there by, "appropriate authorities (Commissions)"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. McCloskey, I couldn't see that section on the ELMO. I see. Yes, sorry. I take that to mean the appropriate government body who would be responsible for the exhumation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so do you have any recollection that the OTP was directing the BiH to a particular body to handle this?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so. And the wording of the document was clear in that section. And, as I say, I authored the document, I can't recall now many of the details, but the document was then processed by the OTP and sent to the Bosnian government with a request that they take responsibility from us for the exhumation of those graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I don't have anything further on that topic. And, now, I'm sure you'll recall that General Tolimir pointed out that Dr. Haglund's report had mentioned a military ID and that -- for 142 Cerska, and that your report mentioned some things but did not mention a military ID. And I wanted to try to put some clarification on that issue. As you recall, you spoke of reviewing various artifacts associated with each of the Cerska bodies and -- such as documents and watches, things like that. And so during that questioning I asked the team to go through the collection, as you'll recall, of the some 2.000 photographs that came from the exhumation and autopsy process that you would have been looking at and provided some of those to the Defence that we thought might be relevant to this issue yesterday when we got them. I doubt the Defence had time to really digest them, but I -- just hopefully we can try to clarify this issue a bit to understand what you were talking about. But if we could first go to your report, which, it should be P -- now, P1825.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go into e-court page 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just very briefly yesterday went through some of the other lists of documents from some of the other graves and would you expect to find that you may have noted military document in some of the other graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sure I would have. If those documents were readable, I would have listed them as what they were or what they had been described by Dr. Haglund's group. So I believe in other graves there is reference to military documents. I seem to recall a military hospital card or a military discharge card in one of the graves. But if I check through the report, I'm sure I would find references to military documents as possible sources of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just take a look at one example. If you can -- it's, I think, three or four lines down. Looking -- it's under the Lazete Orahovac, I think you can see a military document. I don't know if you can read that. It's --

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can read it. Lazete 2, body 007, and Lazete 2, body 010 are listed as having a military document and a military card. I think further down there's also a reference -- sorry, it's a seaman's log, I assume that's a civil seaman's log, but the first two entries are military card and military document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to Mr. Osmo Muminovic, who was Cerska 142, which was the subject of this. That's on just a few pages earlier, on e-court page 98. And what we'll see there is I think what we've gone over before on the first page. If we could blow that up a bit. We'll see under "identification items" for 142, we have a driver's licence for Osmo Muminovic, and under "religious items" we have, for Cerska 142, wooden prayer beads. Now, let me go to just these few photographs that we took or that we found from the vast collection from Cerska that had number 142 on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can now find that in 65 ter 07192 page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, I -- I don't know if the storage -- the way we store photographs now is different than how they were stored when you were looking at them, but looking at this particular image, does, as we see -- can you kind of explain to us what -- do you recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It's a mortuary photograph. The CSK-142 refers to the abbreviation for the Cerska grave. This is body 142. It's item 12 and it's item 12 A. Now, that would indicate to me that item 12 consists of multiple items, and it was probably a wallet, and A is a part of item 12 which was found on body 142. It's a "licna" card, an identity card or a driver's licence. On the top is a translation that's been done at the mortuary. And I indicated that the deterioration of the documents -- in this you can see that the person's photograph is missing. It's faded away. Very often it was the case that when you took the item out of the grave or off the body, the image would disappear as it was exposed to air. We didn't have the facilities to stop that happening. And in any event, as soon as it was disturbed, the document would start very quickly to deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this likely the driver's licence that you were referring to in your report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again we see this is Cerska 142. And the translation up at the top, what does this indicate to you this particular document is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember who would have done these little translations that came with the photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the item was examined at the mortuary, and I think it was in the village of Kladanj at that time, it would be laid out by the scene-of-crime photographer, and I believe that the translation was done by -- was completed by staff employed at the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we don't see an ID card listed in your identification documents, just a driver's licence. Is there any significance to that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I don't know why I didn't list that document. Perhaps because the document itself is unreadable now, or when I examined it, and that that information above could be used for identification purposes, but that the document itself couldn't be looked at, and those details obtained now, because it had deteriorated. But again, that information was included in the greater volume of information for Cerska 142 and was available. But I would suggest that the document itself was unreadable by the time I examined it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, well, we can see clearly a watch. Do you know what these other things are from your experience?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is item 9 from that same body. A watch and a cigarette or a part of a cigarette pipe, and the other box is a tobacco tin; they were very popular. Some of them had names inscribed in them, so we used those as an identification lead. Some had patterns, as I believe this one has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't believe this material made it into the report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, it was a summary, so I had to be brief. It the tin had a name, I would have included it. If the watch was inscribed, I would have included it, probably. But it was simply a summary to show the possible identification avenues open to us. And also I hope that the document that I produced would be of use to agencies like PHR when they're examining this material for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Briefly, what's this?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The black item I'd have to say is a wallet or something like that. I'm not sure. Maybe a religious artifact, you know, in a wallet. The other is a flint and steel for starting fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the wooden beads that I mentioned, that I list as a possible religious affiliation. And, of course, I didn't list the comb. But you can see that they're the artifacts from Cerska 142, that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask, are you sure that the number is CSK-142 or 143? It's really illegible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, you're right. But I'm assuming if it's part of the same series, and if you look at the number in the top right-hand corner, it will indicate that it's the next or subsequent F number. And not only that, there's a photographic log which accompanies this photograph and it would say 142. I'm sure we could check that, or the OTP could check, that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it possible to zoom in just on that part of the ... Oh, it's very difficult. This doesn't help. Okay, Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, that F number is a number which was electronically stamped on the negatives. This was -- this was -- sorry, on the prints. This was film rather than digital so that as they would simply stamp in order each frame. So because I can see that this is 142, the next consecutive frame should certainly be Cerska 142, and it related to the case. And again, there's a log that accompanies it. And it's consistent in that the next item is item 11, where you would expect it to go from Cerska 142, item 1, through to the end of the range of items.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could we just go to the next page again to see what you're talking about. You see item 10 here, 564-21, item 11, 564-22. Okay. Now, we asked -- I asked Mr. Janc to see if he could find any military document that may be associated with Cerska 142, and I have something I want to show you in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In e-court it should be 07193.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Manning, I want to show you the original packet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could have him see this original packet that the records will confirm that Mr. Manning received this on 14 May 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please hand it over. First to the Defence, and then to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is one of the things that I sent an electronic copy to the Defence when we found it yesterday. And we are still waiting for the cover page of that to come up so Your Honours can see just the cover page. And, Your Honours, you may see I've put a little tag on something. That's going to be showing up on the screen with the translation in a minute. It's something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber has had the opportunity to look at these documents. It may be handed over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know it's been many, many years, Mr. Manning, but take a look. We can see that cover page that shows you receiving it, the material, and just take your time to just flip through the material, see if you can have any memory of this sort of stuff at all. And if it will help your recollection, this file was found with a group of five or six others which were actually of men identified on your report, e-court page 96, where PHR had made DNA IDs.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I recognise certainly my signature on the document, on the cover page, and I recognise the type of document. I can't recall receiving this particular document. It is the same as thousands of other packets that I received. It's a normal autopsy record from PHR for that period. And I note towards the back there is a list of documents found, including some details of those documents, including some handwritten notes in relation to those documents, and the tracking sheet which showed the processing of the body and the artifacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to the -- what should be the only other page that was uploaded into e-court. I'm sorry. Page 71. The entire thing is in e-court, I'm sorry. Page 71 is the one that I marked in the red tab and we should have a translation with that if the system is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you'll note, Mr. Manning, before this particular image in the file, there's a couple of other -- appear to be photographs, actually, of items that are similar or the same of some of the photographs that you received from the other that we've just spoken about. But just the simple -- the simple question is, we have here something identified as -- that is readable --

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- that does say "Order," and it's from the War Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated 1992 to Mr. Muminovic, who was 142. And it's basically sending him to be the commander of the guards guarding the -- what we all remember, the big properties down at Zeleni Jadar. So we may have this military document. Now, just to put you on the spot, here is a military document, here is some records that you received, can you -- what -- how can you -- can you explain that for us?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I simply can't. I don't recall physically that packet and item. I note in this packet that it's in the B/C/S language. But, yeah, I accept that there's a military order here and I haven't included it in the document. Perhaps because it says Osmo Muminovic and that's all it says, whereas on the other document I have a date of birth, an address, more material to assist in identification. But I have no idea why that document is not listed. It's listed in Mr. Haglund's report. Perhaps I didn't list it because it really doesn't assist in identifying Osmo Muminovic as much as the other one, but I have no recollection of that and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to direct your attention to the fact that in the report, and this is something that we insisted on in the cross-examination, in Exhibit P1071 on page 65 in the English language, it says "military orders" in the plural. Something that would indicate that there are several military orders. We will agree that what we see on the screen is a military order but is just one military order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have fully searched the material, the photographs that Mr. Manning had received from PHR. That was that first collection; there was no such photograph of this document in it. We did find a photocopied image in this separate file and that's what we have. And that's -- we've been looking for the needle in the haystack and that's what we came up with. There are no other documents, nor do I think it really -- I think we probably exhausted this subject perhaps more than necessary. But it was an interesting topic. We did find the document, so we thought it was appropriate for everyone to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I note that we have two documents on the screen now. Perhaps you can clarify that with the witness, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Manning, His Honour is correct. Do you -- and we can see this thing referred to as "membership card," and there seems to be kind of a vertical separation line between the membership card and the military order. Can you provide any explanation for us?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't recognise it. There were thousands and thousands of documents. I would assume that I didn't list it because it doesn't assist in identifying the victim. And again, my report was a summary and -- but PHR were working on these documents, which is where I got them from, to identify the individuals. And I don't, from memory, know whether the housing co-operative is a military organisation or is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me go to another topic and that is the topic, as we'll recall, General Tolimir said on page 10262: "Since this is Cerska and since there was combat in Cerska before, is it possible that these documents indicate that these victims died in an earlier period, or in a period when Srebrenica fell in July of 1995." And he went on and -- on page 10278, and made a similar statement about this subject and stated: "Since this is very important to the Court, because in 1993 some people were killed in Cerska who might have been killed by other perpetrators and the military documents would show this." And so there's -- and I'm sure you'll remember discussing that with him, the suggestion that the 142 in this grave are from victims of other -- of combat or some other incident previous to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if I could go, on that topic, to 00094 -- sorry, it's P94, page 223.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any -- this is another topic but since we'll on this one we'll skip to it. I'm sure we'll all remember when General Tolimir went over your interview with Mr. Becirovic [sic] where you'd mentioned there was -- you had an aerial photograph of executions, and Judge Nyambe asked you on that same subject. Have you seen this particular image before?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've seen the image before. I'm not familiar with the coloured additions to that image, but I'm very familiar with that image of Branjevo military farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I also have a physical image, Mr. President, that I would like to show the witness which is something to see if he has seen this or a version of it. It's a very -- it's more -- a clearer version of this electronic image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, it may be handed over, but shown to the Defence as well. For the record, Mr. McCloskey, what is depicted in the hard copy of the photograph which is now given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is an identical photograph of -- it's the same photograph as the electronic one but without -- I don't know if we can remember, Mr. Ruez talked about this many months ago. It's identical but it only has the United States' black and white markings on it, without Mr. Ruez's. If you recall, Mr. Ruez explained that he'd reviewed the US material and written in the material that it had stated and that he -- it was also a result of the investigation. And it's all part of that investigation and I just want to ask Mr. Manning if that's one of the things that he might have been thinking of when he made this statement to Mr. Becirovic [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go ahead. But after that, the Chamber would like to see this hard copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the image that I'm referring to, that I believe I was referring to when I spoke to the witness. Not only is it marked on this document, and it says "bodies," my belief that this shows bodies was particularly affected by Mr. Erdemovic's [Realtime transcript read in error "Ademovic's"] testimony which I listened to where he said he stood in an area on this photograph and executed the prisoners and that those shapes were the bodies of those prisoners. That, to me, is the closest thing that we had at that stage to actually a photograph of the executions, a photograph of the murders. You can see that the field is covered with bodies and that there is a mass grave nearby. And when we exhumed the grave, we found a number of bodies. So this is the image or images that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Manning, perhaps you'll recall, or maybe not, that Mr. Erdemovic testified that this occurred for most of the day on 16 July, and this photograph was taken on 17 July. Does that change anything for you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, not really. This is, for me, investigating the genocide, this is tremendous evidence that these men were executed. Whether it happened the day before or the minute before, you see the bodies next to the mass grave with the tracks of the buses and the vehicles. And this is a photo of genocide having immediately taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that perhaps Mr. McCloskey could clarify one thing. What we talked about in P147, which is a conversation between Mr. Manning and the Witness Bircakovic, is the sentence which is on page 19 and which says: We have aerial shots of the executions themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Precisely why I asked -- reminded him that they occurred on the 16th and have asked him if they changed his answer at all, and we heard his answer. So I think I've dealt directly with that issue. But I have no objection to any re-cross or any questions on this, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you done with this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to signal the Registrar to get that photograph up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have that here to the Bench, please. And Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just now, Mr. Manning, you have just said that "... this is tremendous evidence that there were executions ... you see the bodies next to the mass grave ..." Can you mark that for me on the picture on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this area is the area where the bodies are. And this second area -- I'll mark that area 1. And this is the mass grave. I've been to that location. It's not a very large area. And the bodies were within maybe a hundred or more metres to the mass grave that was visible in this image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: And they were still visible when you visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, ma'am. Your Honour, I visited several years later, and these bodies were collected up by machine and placed into the mass grave. The mass grave was sealed and then that mass grave was ultimately robbed or opened up in September and October, and the bodies removed from that -- sorry, a significant number of the bodies were removed from that -- from that grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just one clarification. I have now in front of me the hard copy. It contains some entries in black and white, "piles of earth," "probable bodies," "excavator digging," which are not absolutely identical in their location to that one we have on the screen. And the headline is not Branjevo state farm, but "Mass Burial at Branjevo Farm. Donje Pilica Area, Bosnia-Herzegovina." I would like to know what these black and white inscriptions are, who made them, and -- because it is different from what we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I can try to remind you of Mr. Ruez's testimony and I can also add, of course, as an officer of the court, the -- we received aerial image from the United States in the format of black and white and black and white information, and so all the black and white information that you see on the one on the screen and the document before you is provided by the United States. And they provided -- sometimes they would put different information on that material, but that is fundamentally the same image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Obviously it's the same area depicted in both, but the hard copy in that is only depicted, I would say, the left side of the photograph on the screen, and there's a different title on it in black and white. Therefore, can I take it that these are two different photos from the same location provided by the US government?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I unfortunately cannot -- I can say the United States has provided different scales, different parts of the same place, but 17 July photograph is -- my understanding is fundamentally one photograph. You're seeing it labelled differently. And the coloured labels are Mr. Ruez's version of, as he testified, taking down what he recalled from the United States and his own investigation, having been there. As for -- unfortunately there's -- I have no information nor were we ever provided any about the number of photographs, different, you know, that kind of methods and procedures. But it's my understanding you're looking at an image that is just marked differently or may be a different scale and a different part of the same image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was just asking to have it clear on the record that they are not absolutely identical. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, I would like to reflect on some questions that concern this photograph. We can see something that is marked at the top of the page in the top left-hand side corner. We see something that says "bodies," so we're dealing with bodies. However, you will agree with me that what we can see here are some white and black spots and I'm not convinced whether they are bodies in fact or not. Is there some responsible body or organ that would have clearer images of these bodies in their possession so that I myself could draw the conclusion about whether these are indeed bodies or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, firstly, if I can say, when I saw this image by itself with the label "bodies," I could not accept that they were bodies. They're just shapes. Personally, Mr. Erdemovic stood in -- sat in this court and described those shapes as bodies, and he said he stood to the top of that photograph and shot those people and he gave that evidence. And that convinced me that what I was seeing in this image was indeed bodies. But your question as to the images themselves, I'm aware that they're Rule 70, and I can't provide you with, and I don't know, the answers to those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on several occasions I have heard and I see that it's wrong in the transcript. For example, on page 18, line 12, I believe Mr. Manning was talking about Mr. "Erdemovic" and not Mr. "Ademovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, would you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Erdemovic. E-r-d-o-m-v-i-c. Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We best offer this into evidence before I forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, this marked photograph on the screen, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1931, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, in relation to the -- Mr. Ruez's conclusion that these were bodies and the United States government which --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For Your Honours, we are certainly not suggesting that it's the United States's government conclusion that proves this assertion, so just so that's clear. It's one element in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall from the investigation the statements or testimony of the two survivors of this mass execution?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours. I can't recall the names, but I recall reading their statements and listening to their testimony or to the testimony of some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's part of the record, so I won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it might have to do with the translation or something, but what was done in cross-examination is from P547 [as interpreted], page -- where the witness said: [In English] "We have aerial images of the executions taking place." [Interpretation] Which indicates that Mr. Manning told the witness that they had aerial shots of the executions themselves, of the executions happening. And what we're dealing with here is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was Exhibit P147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gajic, but this is the way the re-examination is conducted by Mr. McCloskey. And at the end of the day we have to consider if everything is consistent or not. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no objection for a request for re-cross to bring up the issues, but making the argument at this point is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you -- again, this is a memory test. Do you remember the -- any shell casings being picked up by the investigators in those early years before you got here and where they picked up shell casings?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have to check my report, but it was consistent with the shell casings being located where the bodies -- or nearby where the bodies are indicated on this photograph. I'd have to check the report. But it was consistent with Mr. Erdemovic's testimony and the survivors' accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just in looking at the photograph, do you -- whoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go back to where it used to be so we can -- could you perhaps blow that up a little bit for us in the area marked "bodies."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see something marked "excavator digging" which -- but do you see any marks on the ground that look at all identifiable to you in this area?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I indicated before that I could see the tracks of vehicles. I was aware that the people had been brought into the farm in buses and that there was heavy machinery there to dig the mass grave. And I believe you can clearly see tracks leading to where the bodies are, then round to the mass grave. And as I said before, based on Mr. Erdemovic's testimony and what I had seen, initially I couldn't accept that they were bodies because you can only see shapes, but later on I certainly believed that they were bodies, and that this image and that other image that you have before you are aerial images of, in my opinion, an execution which has just taken place in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was waiting for the end of the answer. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise for not switching the microphone on. The Defence has repeatedly tried to draw your attention to a relevant issue. What is being discussed here goes beyond the scope of cross-examination and I don't know why this is allowed to go on despite numerous well-intended comments on our part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think I'm through with this. And it was actually -- the General was correct in that it was originally designed to -- for Mr. Manning to be able to tell us what meant when he was interviewing or interrogating Mr. Becirovic [sic]. But, of course, it was His Honour's natural interest and questions in this document and whether or not they're bodies that led us to these questions, so I think it's of course absolutely appropriate that it's gone this far, but it's -- I have no further questions on this particular topic, and I'm ready to go to the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to note Mr. Gajic, you gave the right reference to the part of the cross-examination Mr. McCloskey is referring to. It's exactly dealing with this question. Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, let me try to go to Cerska, and that is the same, but page 62 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should give Mr. Gajic the opportunity to say something to the last topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, again we have a name misspelled. On page 21, line 22, it says Mr. "Becirovic," whereas I think it should state "Bircakovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, are you referring in your statement to Mr. Bircakovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I may have mixed the names up, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you need your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I may have mixed the names up. I was referring to the person on cross-examination, and I think it was Bircakovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is really a good co-operation between the parties. Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go now to P94, page 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we wait for that, do you recall seeing any aerial images -- well, there it is.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm familiar with this image. It's a split-pane image, if you like, before and after. Before on the left, and after on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to remind the Court, I'm back on the re-cross -- the re-direct subject of whether or not this -- the victim in this grave was a battle casualty from prior to the Srebrenica events, as I'd set out in line and page in two places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what -- does this image give us any indication of the date the Cerska grave was created?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, it's a window. So on the 5th of July, 1995, there's no disturbance at the grave-site. As of the 27th of July, there's a clear disturbance. It's exactly the same area. You can see the roadway down to the -- from the centre of the photo to the right where the road splits. It's exactly the same area, and it shows the grave which has been created, which was maybe a year later exhumed by the ICTY PHR team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think you had described that -- could you briefly describe how -- your understanding on how the victims were shot and ...

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was a witness account of buses travelling to the area, followed by an APC and, I believe, a heavy machine, a digging machine. On examination by the archaeologists, I think 140-something bodies were located, underneath soil, a thin later of soil, which had been taken from the side of the road. The men had been shot in -- at the site and either fallen or rolled down a slight embankment on the road. Soil had been scooped from the other side of the road and dumped across the bodies. It was a shallow cover of soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you see anything on this particular image that would indicate any taking from soil to be used in this burial process?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe what you see is on the right-hand pane, there's a large oval shape --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we blow that up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within that oval shape, if you look on the right-hand side, a smaller rectangle, and then a larger rectangle on the other side of the road. The soil has been taken from the small rectangle, scooped up from the bank, and then dumped on the bodies on the left-hand rectangle and then spread over the bodies. It was described by Dr. Haglund as a thin layer of soil on top of the bodies. And in the photographs just prior to exhumation, you can see that there are pieces of clothing and, very often in mass graves, shoes on the surface or partially exposed on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you been to this very site yourself?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have. But it was exhumed in 1996 and I didn't visit it until 1998. And I visited many occasions or travelled through the area. All you can see now is a dirt road and a piece of disturbed soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the same topic regarding battle casualties prior to this event, could we go to 65 ter 07192, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you are asking for another 65 ter number. You have used already two of those documents, 65 ter 7192 and -93 but you didn't tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, this is page 1 of, actually, 7192. So it was the last one. I haven't used that yet. And I -- this should be the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, we see these red numbers in the right, we see Cerska 142. Before we get into the image itself, what -- what is this?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to see, but it's, I believe, an exhumation photograph. It's listed as Cerska 142, the individual we've been talking about. It's very difficult to see from this, but I believe it pictures the body in the mass grave. I have seen this image before. I examined every image taken from this grave and every other mass grave at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you make out the position of the body in this at all?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps it's the light, but I believe the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I just look to make sure he's got the same image I do? It's very difficult for the witness to see it. I couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have had such a situation earlier in this trial. Yes, this would help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, very much, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To have another angle. Or you could please rise for a moment and look more from the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you can see, if I may, here is the individual's foot. And the rest of the body moves up towards the top of the image. Now, if you see the plastic -- the black plastic bag in this area --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Better number those.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In area 2, it may be that this is an image at the mortuary. What would normally happen is the body would be collected - Cerska grave was particularly wet and muddy - the body would be taken to the morgue, the first photograph taken would be of the body-bag laid on the floor and opened up. And this may be a mortuary photograph. I would have expected the label to be slightly different at the mortuary. But it shows the condition of body 142 from Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you make out anything related to the arms and their positions?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it shows the arms in a fairly classic position behind the back, bound. I would have to check the image.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I better tender this since we have some markings on it. And I should tender the images from 07192 that we've already talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be received as an exhibit. And as another exhibit, this marked photograph we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- marked photograph will be received as Exhibit P1932 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I do apologise. Your Honours, marked photograph will be received as Exhibit P1932. And 65 ter 07192 will be given Exhibit P1933. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Staying on this same topic, could we go to Exhibit P1315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you, in the meantime, what about the 65 ter 7193?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the military document. That should be entered as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1934, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We need P1315. And page 15 -- 50, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Manning, what is this, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a autopsy report produced by the physicians for human rights ICTY exhumations team in the 1996 exhumations process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is the case of number 142, Mr. Muminovic, that we're speaking of; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cerska 142, yes. No name at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Correct. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is in evidence, Your Honours, but I just briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is -- is this a fairly typical description of the clothing and the personal effects?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Particularly the clothing. That was a source of identification, so they did try to describe the clothing as well as they could. And, in fact, once the body was recovered, the pathologist looked at the clothing for signs of injury, as in bullet strikes, then the body. And then they removed the clothing from the body, washed it, and then photographed it and described it. And in relation to the personal effects, that's similar to the descriptions used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to the next page of the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we look at the identification papers, we see the driver's licence and we see a reference to other papers related to the military responsibilities of Osmo Muminovic. Is that the material that we've seen before on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd accept that, that it would be listed in Mr. Haglund's report, it would be listed in this document, and it would be listed in the photographic logs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we see the external examination, skin characteristics. Nothing I want to point out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see the description of the trauma. I won't go -- though, as I realise, there is not a B/C/S version of this, so -- but we just -- we can see, in English, number 1 talks about damage to the pelvis; number 2 is absence of facial skeleton; number 3 is fracture or loss of bone fragments; number 4, something medical I don't quite understand; number 5, some damage to ribs; number 6, fracture of femur of post-mortem appearance; and then other damage to other parts of the body. But recovered evidence, this is what I want to ask you about. Projectiles: bullet, one from the right elbow; bullet, one from the left thigh; bullet jacket, one from the central chest; bullets, two from the central upper chest; bullet, one from the left shoulder; bullet, one from the chest wall; bullet fragment, one from the left chest wall; bullet, one from the left axilla. And then other evidence - the tobacco tin, the watch - we've seen. And if we go to the next page, here we see at the top the prayer beads and a green plastic wallet with various documents. And under "cause of death," "head injury consistent with gun-shot wound with injuries to pelvis, chest, and limbs compatible with fire-arms injuries." Is this -- particularly these -- the presence of these bullets and these injuries about the body, is that consistent with the investigative theory of this being a mass execution as you've described?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is. Again, I'm not a pathologist, but it's certainly consistent with what I indicated, was that these men were murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And one last document, P01782.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous page shown, of the document we have on our screens. Witness, in reference to the part of the document dealing with bullets, projectiles, mention is made of several bullets. Were these bullets found on the individual himself or were they recovered in the mass grave as such, in the grave-site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, from this document, which is created by the pathologists in the mortuary, this indicates to me - and I've read all of these documents - that they were actually physically recovered from the body. In the Cerska grave, the bodies were almost completely fleshed so that the bullets were removed from the flesh of the individual and the bones. In this instance, "bullet 1 from right elbow" indicates that that was actually physically removed from the body itself. Again, the thigh, the chest, the shoulder, the chest wall, these bullets and bullet fragments would be identified from x-ray fluoroscope. They would be identified by the pathologist looking at the clothing and seeing a hole through the clothing and then, underneath the clothing, a hole in the body. The body was then -- the clothing was taken and the bullet was recovered from the flesh of the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: During the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the autopsy process. And, Your Honours, the fluoroscope images, the x-ray images, would clearly show the skeleton of the body, the flesh of the body, and the very bright marks of the bullet, so they would know that they would need to recover those items and they would describe those items in the document where they were found in this case within the body itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was waiting for interpretation. Because my calculation came down to some nine bullets, so you confirm that these nine bullets were found on this one corpse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. I might indicate that - one, two - the item number 3, "bullet jacket 1 from central chest," indicates that the bullet had a cover and then a core, and the cover of the bullet has come off. So to be completely correct, it could be that that bullet jacket is a part of one of the other bullets. But certainly that indicates nine bullets or parts of bullets were removed from that body. Where it says "bullet jacket," that's a large part of the bullet; and where it says "bullet fragment," that could be a part of one of the other bullets. So at the very least you would have seven or eight separate bullets within that body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just on that, do you recall the most common calibre of bullet that was found?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost overwhelmingly .762. There were some unusual rounds, some shot-gun pellets and the odd larger bullets, but predominantly .762.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then this one last exhibit, P01782.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you familiar with this cover sheet? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's the Book of the Dead, the ICTY count of the Srebrenica missing, and I note that it's from May of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we go to page 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you look at the fourth person down.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that Cerska 142?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but I can't see the "Cerska," and you wouldn't, the grave reference. I would check the BAZ number, which is an ICMP PHR number, but I believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And under the date and place of disappearance, what would that -- what would that indicate to you as to his relationship to any of these events?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's information provided by, if you like, the last person who saw him alive, and where. And indicates the 11th of July, 1995. Last seen in the forests near Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, this concludes your examination here in this trial. The Chamber would like to thank you that you were able to provide us with your knowledge. And now you are free to return to your normal activities. Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate your good wishes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's the right time for our first break now. We will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderpuye. Is the next witness ready for his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone. Yes, Mr. President, the next witness is ready. I just want to bring two matters to your attention. The first is with respect to the re-direct examination of Dr. Helge Brunborg. As you recall, it was last Thursday, I had indicated that we intended to conduct a re-direct examination of him. Having reviewed the record quite carefully and discussed with my colleagues on the team, we've decide that a further examination of Dr. Brunborg is not necessary. So unless the Trial Chamber has certain important issues which requires him to be brought back for the Trial Chamber, I'd ask at this point for him to be discharged, if that's necessary in a formal way. I understand also that General Tolimir has completed his cross-examination of Dr. Brunborg as he indicated previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates your reconsideration of the situation in respect of Dr. Brunborg. I think it is very fortunate that he must not travel the third time to The Hague. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The second issue I wanted to raise is with respect to the witness that's going to testify today. I've been in contact with Mr. Gajic, in particular concerning a document that was brought to our attention by Dr. Parsons and it concerns an independent review of the technical processes related to the DNA processes used by the ICMP and its a report that's dated April 14th of 2010. I obtained a copy of that report from Dr. Parsons, which I sent to Mr. Gajic the very day that I got it. It is in the process of being translated. A partial and incomplete translation - I shouldn't say partial; a draft, rather - and incomplete translation was sent to Mr. Gajic just within an hour or so ago. And we are in the process of trying to translate it. I understand that we are -- that the Defence is prepared to proceed. They will obviously need to evaluate this document. And to the extent that they might require additional time to do so or to have Mr. -- Dr. Parsons return, we are certainly fine with that. But I am prepared to proceed with the direct examination, and I think that a fair amount of cross-examination can be accomplished notwithstanding -- notwithstanding their recent -- that is, the Defence's recent receipt of this document. I should add, also, that it's not on my exhibit list. I have no intension to elicit information concerning this document from the witness. So I think I'll leave it to Mr. Gajic if he chooses to respond, but I've discussed it with him in advance of the sitting this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do have a very brief summary of Dr. Parsons's testimony that I'd like to read into the record just to familiarise the Court with the basic substance of his testimony. If I may proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons is the director of forensic sciences for the International Commission for Missing Persons, which operates a highly experienced DNA laboratory system, active since 2001. In October 2007, the organisation received an ISO 17025 accreditation, which is one of the most significant international accreditation standards governing forensic DNA analysis. The mandate of the organisation is the identification of missing persons. And its task is principally three fold: One, to assist governments with the issue of missing persons through governmental relations and that is to work with governments to establish laws and policies and to hold them accountable for the problem of the missing. Two is to conduct a civil society initiative to mobilise family groups and provide them with the ability to meet and with the -- to meet and with funding so that they can have a voice in the government. And three is to provide forensic assistance by way of DNA identification. The ICMP is not a law enforcement organisation. And it operates independently. As director of forensic sciences at the time of his testimony, Dr. Parsons was responsible for, among other things, supervising three forensic science divisions within the organisation. In particular, the examinations and excavations division, which conducts anthropological and pathological analysis; the DNA laboratory system, which handles DNA typing, in order to match DNA profiles obtained from bone to blood samples; and the DNA identification and co-ordination division, which establishes links between samples and genetic data. Dr. Parsons testified regarding the DNA testing procedures and protocols applied by the ICMP. He explained the nature and the reliability of DNA testing in general as well as the specific processes applied by the ICMP. In particular, Dr. Parsons underscored that the ICMP applies nuclear STR typing, which is a technology that is validated and accepted within the scientific community, fully meeting industry standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is an extremely well established standard that has emerged in forensic diagnosis. He noted also that it is a technology widely used in both the United Kingdom and in the United States. In addition, as part of its accreditation, the ICMP is subject to a formal review process and technical audits are carried out. Several standard operating procedures document the manner in which the ICMP carries out its DNA testing. These standard operating procedures reflect established fundamental science and procedures shared with other DNA laboratories. Many of them are expressly referred to and explained in Dr. Parsons methodology report, covering the period from 2001 through 2008. Dr. Parsons noted that there have been minor procedural changes over time relating to changes in the primary instrumentation that's used to newer more sensitive equipment. While this increased the success rate, that is, the ability to extract DNA, it did not affect the fundamental reliability of the techniques applied. The ICMP's DNA matching procedure is robust, documented, and regulated. In essence, this is the process of comparing the DNA taken from a bone sent to the ICMP for testing against the database of DNA profiles obtained from blood samples provided by donors. The issuance of a match report, which is simply the result of a DNA test, requires a minimum threshold of statistical surety of 99.95 per cent. In cases where there is presumptive evidence of identity, for example, such as the presence of artifacts, match reports are issued with 99 per cent statistical surety. The ICMP also has a formal system of review for all DNA reports. Dr. Parsons testified that the ICMP does not issue death certificates; rather, local pathologists deal with this process. As such, a case is considered closed when the court-appointed pathologist by the Bosnian national authorities issues a death certificate and returns the remains to the family members. Nevertheless, as of his 2009 testimony, 6.006 individuals connected to Srebrenica-related mass graves had been identified through ICMP's DNA identification efforts. That concludes my summary, Mr. President. And I do have a number of questions yet to put to Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, it's been almost two years since you testified last here. Can you tell us, what are some of the more significant things you've been doing since you testified last?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, of course we've been continuing in a highly energetic programme of scientific technical assistance to the identification process in the former Yugoslavia, state of Bosnia. Continuing our work with high throughput DNA analysis and comparing bone samples, DNA profiles obtained from bone samples of victims, to large databases of family reference blood profiles in order to make matches, and this keeps us very busy. Moreover, a principal element of my job is to make sure that we stay current with best practices and advancements in the field. And when improvements in methodology become -- when we become aware of improvements in methodology, either through the scientific literature or our own experimentation, we'll validate those procedures and implement them into our casework. So in terms of the biggest changes we've made, one is, I think you've referred to earlier, just having to do with the state-of-the-art instrumentation. The companies that make these high-tech instruments release improved models, and we have followed along with developments in that field, so we've validated new sets of instruments. It doesn't materially change the nature of the testing very much. Another thing that has been among the biggest changes is a new DNA extraction method that we have developed from bone samples that we've been able to demonstrate provides a greater likelihood of successfully obtaining a DNA profile from a bone sample. And I'll just give a moment of background to say that these samples have been environmentally challenged. They're beneath soil, mixed in with other grave -- with other bodies in the grave, a lot of microbial activity, et cetera, and this is -- this can degrade bone -- the DNA surviving in with the bone sample, so it's important to have chemical techniques that are very effective at removing the surviving DNA molecules from the bone matrix, making them available to the testing process. And so our new DNA typing method -- DNA extraction method has been validated, implemented, and -- as well as published in the literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind you to speak a little more slowly because it is very difficult for the interpreters to catch everything what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
