utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will try to revisit some of these issues a little bit more in detail as we go along. But, first, I'd like to put -- I'd like to show you what's marked here as 65 ter 7190. This is a copy of your CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't think we have a translation of this yet. We do? Okay. Great.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think this is a copy of your most recent CV. Do you recognise that, Dr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just in terms of your responsibilities with the ICMP, are they fundamentally the same or have they changed in any way from what they were when you last testified?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: They are fundamentally the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of your activities -- let me pause for a moment. In terms of your activities with the organisation, can you tell us have you engaged in any new conferences, written any new papers that are reflected on your CV?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, there are a number of additional publications since we last would have met, and those would be listed much further down in the document, where publications are listed. With regard to conferences and that type of professional outreach, I would comment that the ICMP is very much a player in the global forensic community. We very frequently attend professional conferences, both to present our work as well as to be sure that we are staying up with the recent developments in the field. I routinely attend meetings of the European Network of Forensic Science Institutes where, again, we are -- we work very closely with our colleagues, so that our work is very well known in its details and actually is very highly regarded internationally as among the most successful human identification programmes. Last year at the American Academy of Forensic Science meetings in Seattle, we presented a mini-symposium of 12 separate scientific lectures to a large audience, detailing all aspects of the scientific work we do with regard to the 1995 fall of Srebrenica and subsequent identifications and investigations that we have performed. And this was -- this was extremely well received by the scientific community.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you participated in authoring or reviewing articles concerning the identification processes that the ICMP has engaged in since the time that you last testified?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. I would have to check the CV to recall the number of those. But, yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't want to go through that because I can -- I'm going to move to admit it into evidence, Mr. President, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I tried to figure out if it's in your list of documents to be used. I doubt it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I haven't actually -- I'm sorry, I have it listed here as the fourth item in the first category of -- the third item in the first category of material, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was just updated by the Registry. I had a previous list and not the current one. Thank you. This CV will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1937, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, is the ICMP's role limited to the identification of the missing as a result of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia or is it more expansive than that? If you could tell us a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. As a result of the unparalleled success that we have demonstrated in our work in the former Yugoslavia, we have become more globally involved in mostly DNA identification efforts. So we currently, or in the past, have responded to requests for assistance in a number of global events, such as the South-East Asian Thailand tsunami. We performed victim DNA typing on all samples related to Hurricane Katarina in the United States. We've assisted INTERPOL in large-scale DNA identification with regard to a ferry sinking in the Philippines. And we have been contracted by the Government of Chile to assist in the human rights violation missing persons casework regarding disappearances in 1973. As examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in respect of the ICMP's involvement in those particular areas, has it always been limited to the subject matter of forensic DNA testing or does it participate in these efforts in other capacities?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, yes. In fact, in these proceedings there tends to be an emphasis on the forensic aspects of ICMP's work and the DNA typing, but ICMP is not fundamentally a forensic organisation. We have a great deal of experience in assisting governments with many facets of taking responsibility of the issue of missing persons. So from that standpoint, for example, the ICMP was invited to perform a comprehensive analysis of the missing persons issues in the country of Colombia, and we sent our teams of experts to look at those issues, including forensic issues such as anthropology and DNA identification but also covering aspects of civil society, victim's rights, legal structure, accountability, reparations, that type of thing. All these are areas where the ICMP has a great deal of expertise and perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you may have heard me mention, during the course of the summary, about -- concerning your prior testimony that the ICMP is an independent organisation. Can you tell us a bit about that. Can you tell us, first, a little bit about how the organisation came into being.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP was established in 1996 through a joint initiative at a G7 Conference. So it's a product of a international initiative that was originally, I think, championed foremost by former president Bill Clinton of the United States. And that -- so that's how the ICMP became established, specifically with a mandate for the former Yugoslavia. In the course of our work, we are, indeed, a fully independent entity, independent of any government and certainly independent of any corporation or external influence. The ICMP is overseeing in broad stroke by a set of prominent commissioners; the current chairman -- chairperson of the ICMP, of the commission, is James Kimsey, an international philanthropist, if you will. And a number of other prominent international individuals make up the commission. We enjoy diplomatic privileges and immunities in our headquarter agreements in Bosnia and therefore are able to provide assurances of data protection and independence as we -- as we go through our work for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does the ICMP have what might be called a steering committee with respect to forensic sciences in particular?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. Almost since the inception of the forensic programmes, the ICMP has, again, sought to ensure maximal transparency as well as advice from leaders in the field. So early on, this body was referred to as a scientific advisory board. And I became familiar with the ICMP because of my role on the scientific advisory board. At that time I was the chief scientist of the DNA identification lab of the United States Armed Forces and came to sit on the scientific advisory board, where experts in the fields of anthropology, forensic archaeology, pathology, statistical analysis, DNA typing, and those kind of things would meet on an annual basis at the ICMP for a multi-day exposure to the overall system. They were able to see everything we do and ask questions and evaluate. And we would pose our greatest challenges to this group and seek their advice on how we could best -- best meet the challenges that we're facing. This advisory group has now referred to differently; we call it the Forensic Science Steering Committee, but it does continue to meet to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about what the advisory committee or government -- or of government representatives is, if you know, as concerns the role of the ICMP in government-related affairs?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not quite sure what committee you're referring to, if it's different than the one I've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm referring to a different committee. Denoted as the Advisory Committee of Government Representatives. Is there such a committee?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not aware of a committee that goes by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in terms of the role of the Steering Committee, does that have anything to do with the kinds of cases that the ICMP becomes involved in? Or is that determination made at another level or by another body?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, the Steering Committee, the Forensic Science Steering Committee is wholly advisory and it doesn't really play a role in the type of engagements the ICMP would or would not be involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the process by which the decision to engage in one area or another is made in the ICMP, that is, whether you're involved in a plane crash in Cameroon, whether you're involved in Katrina, a ferry sinking in the Philippines, and so on, how is that determination made?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It almost always refers back to our general mandate of assisting governments with regard to the issue of missing persons. And we would typically respond at the invitation of a government for assistance. And in instances, I'll say also, that we have made offers of assistance - for example, with regard to Katarina - and our capabilities, we would -- we'd make ourselves available and then the government would then request our help.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit about the facilities that the ICMP operates. Where, currently, are your facilities located?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The headquarters and primary DNA testing laboratory is in Sarajevo, Bosnia. Another forensic unit is the identification co-ordination division, and that's located in Tuzla, Bosnia. We have a component of the DNA laboratory system housed in Banja Luka in the Republika Srpska of Bosnia. And all the samples that are tested for DNA also go through a process in that specialised Banja Luka facility. Associated with the ICMP for a long time has been a facility also in Tuzla called the Podrinje Identification Project. This is a mortuary facility where remains specific to Srebrenica are stored and evaluated, and that is headed by a court-appointed forensic pathologist with official capacity in the Bosnian court system. And he in the past has also been a member of the ICMP, basically wearing two hats. And this PIP, we call it, Podrinje Identification Project, was established by the ICMP but in very recent months has been fully transferred in authority over to the Bosnian national authorities, although we do continue to provide technical assistance through the action of some of our expert forensic anthropologists and other staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does the ICMP maintain regional offices in Belgrade and Pristina, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I believe that the Belgrade office is no longer in operation, but we do have an office in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And during the course of the identification processes that took place with respect to the Srebrenica missing, at any point did the ICMP maintain a region office in Belgrade, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Not only a region office, but we had a division of our DNA laboratory system in Belgrade that assisted primarily with some of the DNA typing from family reference samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Approximately how many DNA laboratories does the ICMP operate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Presently we have just two that are involved in the DNA process; that's the DNA laboratory in Banja Luka in Republika Srpska and the main laboratory in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the identification co-ordination division that you referred to, can you tell us, does that operate from one of the DNA facilities, or is that a separate facility? If you could just explain what its role is and how it's situated in the organisation.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It is a separate facility from the DNA laboratories, but it's absolutely integral in the process. The identification co-ordination division is located in Tuzla, and that is the facility where all samples that we obtain are received by the ICMP. Bone samples that have been submitted from the graves, from whatever external submitter, as well as blood samples that are received from family members of the missing, enter the ICMP system at the identification co-ordination division. And they're immediately stripped of any identifiers regarding where they come from and entered into an electronically tracked barcoded system so that all processes downstream, in terms of the DNA laboratory testing, et cetera, are done in a fully objective and blind manner. So all samples appear identical with regard to their processing in the laboratory. The other place where the identification co-ordination centre plays a very strong role is that after the DNA laboratory system has performed a test and obtained a profile associated with either a victim or a family reference sample, those DNA profiles are submitted to the identification co-ordination centre where sophisticated computer matching is done that finds a relationship between the victim bone sample and a family reference sample. And it is the identification co-ordination division that then generates the DNA match reports that indicate a strong statistical association, thereby essentially naming the individual from whom a bone sample comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll have you walk us through the identification process in a just a moment. With respect to the mortuary facilities that you refer to, can you tell us how many mortuary facilities are involved in the ICMP's DNA identification efforts? As relates to Srebrenica missing, in particular, if you can distinguish between them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please make a pause between question and answer for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe I can repeat my question. I'm sorry about that. With respect to the mortuary facilities, can you tell us how many are involved in the process -- in ICMP's DNA identification process concerning Srebrenica related?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Presently, the ICMP operates only a single mortuary facility with direct relevance to Srebrenica, and that's the PIP facility I mentioned earlier. Historically, additional facilities have been involved, both under ICMP control and under control of other agencies, such as the ICTY itself, involved in the exhumation process. The ICMP in previous years operated a facility near Visoko and also had a specialised subset or sub-unit of PIP called the Lukavac Reassociation Centre. And that was located in the town of Lukavac, which is very close to Tuzla in Bosnia, and was a specialised facility for examination of extremely fragmented and co-mingled remains that were -- that had been exhumed from secondary mass graves that pose a very serious challenge to an identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you would, I'd like you to walk us through the process of identification in a bit of a nutshell because part of it is in your prior testimony. But can you tell us, basically, how the process starts. You've mentioned that somebody will come in and report a family member missing. Can you tell us what happens following that.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, there are basically two lines to the process. One involving recovery examination, sampling, and DNA typing of victim samples that come from, generally speaking, mass graves. And the other relating to the family reporting of family members that are missing and the provision of blood samples in order to make identifications. So I'll spend just a few sentences to expanded on both of those. And I'll start with the family reference sample collection. This is a result of a huge programme of outreach by the ICMP to make it known to the families that are -- have people missing from the conflict that they can participate in the identification of their loved one by registering this person as a missing -- their loved one as a missing person with the ICMP and providing blood samples that allow us to generate DNA profiles. So this is done in a very, very large manner. We currently have some 70.000 family reference blood samples relating only to the state of Bosnia, and these reflect the report of missing of some 23.000 missing persons in the state of Bosnia. And this has been a process that is implemented by a great deal of communication to the families, the organisation of family groups, providing them with information, and understanding from them, in the course of dialogue, what their needs are and what their situation is. So I'm just trying to indicate that we have a great deal of interaction with families and that has been the basis for the extreme success we've had in obtaining so many samples from missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, I would appreciate if you could speak more slowly. It's very difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, would you like me to repeat any of that more slowly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see everything was recorded properly. But for the interpreters it takes a long time to interpret to different languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. So when the blood samples are obtained from the family with appropriate genetic -- with appropriate consent to provide those samples, and assurances that they will be used only for the purposes of identifying their loved ones, those samples are then typed for a DNA profile and entered into a missing persons DNA profile database, also associated with information regarding how that individual is related to the victim and other contact information regarding the family members and the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned that an individual would come in and essentially report a family member missing as a result of a massive outreach programme by the ICMP. Do you know at -- whether at the time that individuals are reported missing to the ICMP, or is there any screening process to determine whether or not these individuals have reported missing family members to other organisations such as the ICRC or any other agencies operating in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: There is a great deal of overlap between individuals that are reported to us as missing and the lists that are maintained by organisations such as the ICRC, yes. The -- the unique distinction of our database is its linkage to blood samples and therefore genetic samples. So for each person we have in our database, we also have genetic profiles associated with family members from that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a great deal of overlap. Is that to suggest that the list that the ICRC might have is not co-extensive with the list that the ICMP may have?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct. There has not been a formal process of reconciliation of those lists. And furthermore, they exist for slightly different purposes. Ours is primarily designed with regard to the ability to identify these missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the collection of blood samples you indicated that, relevant information concerning the donors' relation to the victim, is taken down, can you tell us - and we'll get to this, I think, a little bit more when we talk about the type of testing you do, but, generally, what kind of relationship are you looking for between a donor and a victim in order to make a reliable DNA match or identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, the most useful donor reference sample comes from a first-degree relative, such as a mother or a father or an offspring. Other combinations of relatives can also be quite definitive for an identification. And we get many different pedigrees, if you will, that we use. So in many instances we may have a mother and two siblings. Ideally is a father and a mother, and that is essentially sufficient to be certain you'll make an identification. And then other constellations of relatives can be quite sufficient for making a DNA match. One thing to understand is that whether one can find a match of suitable -- of sufficient statistical surety depends on the genetic types of the family involved. Now, we look at a number of different independent nuclear DNA loci - these are simply different positions within the chromosomes of an individual - that vary independently of one another. And at any one of these locations you can have a type - I can expand on that later, if need be - but that type can either be common in the population or very rare in the population. So if a family has types at a particular genetic locus - that's one of these positions I'm referring to - that's very rare, then it's going to be easier to identify the loved one of that individual because he will share that rare type. So we'll have some instances -- all this is to say, we'll have some instances where a mother, based on the genetic types that she has, as well as her offspring, will allow, basically, a certain identification, 99.9999999 per cent surety, and other instances where, if this type -- if this family is mostly common genetic types, where the mother may not be sufficient in and of herself to allow us to be even 99.95 per cent sure, and that's why we always attempt to get multiple family members as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned the collection -- well, I should say, rather, the analysis of bone samples, which are, for all intents and purposes, extracted from exhumed bodies. Can you tell us a bit about the process by which these bone samples come to your lab, and then, separately, about what happens to the bone samples once they get to your lab.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, the bone samples can come to our lab from any number of means. For the purposes of the Court, it's probably most useful to focus on what is the vast, vast majority of our cases, which would be human remains exhumed from mass graves of various sizes. With regard to Srebrenica, very often these mass graves are very large. And also are what are known as secondary mass graves, where the assemblage of individuals has been moved from the primary grave and trucked off to a different site and then reburied again in a clandestine site. So with regard to samples received by the ICMP, they could come from remains that were exhumed by the ICTY in early years, post-conflict. They could also come, and this is a very common category, from exhumations where the ICMP played a role in the process. So we have teams of highly expert forensic anthropologists and forensic archaeologists, and around the period of 2000 or so, the ICMP began to provide technical assistance at exhumations. So the process would be mediated -- the official process of an exhumation would be through a court order and the action of a joint exhumation project. And this is a system put in place by the Office of the High Representative in 1996 whereby the Bosnian Croat Federation Missing Persons Commission would work together with the Republika Srpska Missing Persons Office to conduct excavations. So in the case of Srebrenica, where the ICMP became involved in technical assistance, the site would be opened up through this joint exhumation process, where the primary team involved would be the Bosnian Croat Federation Missing Persons Commission, and they would be conducting the auspices of the excavation, supervised in most instances by a representative of the Republika Srpska office, as well as by security provided 24 hours a day by the Republika Srpska Police. In many of these instances, the ICMP has provided a wide range of technical assistance. But in many instances, full technical assistance with regard to the conduct of forensic archeological excavation, where state-of-the-art methods of stratographic recovery of human remains were applied with positional -- electronic positional data collection, to maintain a very solid archive of all the human remains and evidentiary material that was removed from the site. And one of the things that's very important in exhuming these complex mass graves, particularly the secondary mass graves where the bodies have become fragmented and co-mingled by this movement process, is the application of anthropological expertise so that you don't just go in and pull out a whole pile of bones. You go in and you remove the portions of individuals that are articulated in a way so that you don't make the grave a greater jumble than it already is. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just -- if I could, I'm sorry. I just want to ask you, you mentioned the Office of the High Representative and its role as concerns joint exhumation, the joint exhumation process. Could you just tell what the Office of the High Representative is to your understanding, just so that we have a clear record on that matter.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I beg the Court's indulgence in my lack of expertise regarding the political structures. I will admit to really being mostly a scientist. But my understanding of the Office of the High Representative is that this is a body that has been established by the Peace Implementation Council, I think it is. At any rate, it's an international representative that is in place to basically -- as a result of the Dayton Peace Accords, if I'm correct. And please, I don't know this in detail. But this is a body with high powers, high administrative powers, in Bosnia that is capable of executing administrative authority in time of need. Generally, the political system in Bosnia is designed to operate itself, but this is a mechanism by which the international community in association with the peace accord has an administrative oversight role that they can exercise. And that's the best I can do with that answer. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of the sample -- the samples that are received by the ICMP, is the ICMP responsible, does it have any influence, over the way these samples are marked or labelled, and in particular in respect of their relationship to any mass grave in particular or any exhumation site in particular?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The general answer to that question is no. Depending on who is involved in the process of sampling -- of examining the remains and sampling them for DNA, we would get any type of labelling convention. It is the case that the ICMP itself has conventions that it prefers to see applied, and we would encourage people to use those. And when the entire process is under our control, these very widely-applied nomenclature systems for sample labelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In a nutshell, does the ICMP operate, at least the forensic laboratories, operate as would a laboratory that was conducting an ordinary blood test, for example? If somebody went to see their doctor and blood was drawn and it was sent off to be tested, does it operate along similar principles?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, insofar as we conduct an accredited, uniform, and highly regarded testing -- expert testing system, I think that the overall process would operate very much like that. That there's a biological sample that requires a scientific analysis to be performed on it and samples are submitted and then a test result is turned back. I won't --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there any selectivity on the part of the ICMP in terms of the samples that it receives? In other words, does it have any influence over the source or type of samples, bone samples, that it receives to compare against the donor blood profiles that it receives?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP does have influence over what it receives but does not always have control over what it receives. There are many instances where the physical remains that are recovered from the graves are transferred to ICMP facilities, and the anthropological examination and DNA sampling takes place within our control there. And under those circumstances, we have highly evolved sampling protocols that are designed to minimise the amount of DNA testing necessary, while maximizing the ability to properly re-associate disassembled remains. So what that means is that we have a standard operating procedure on recommendations for sites on the skeleton that should be sampled for DNA. And we've made those -- that standard operating procedure widely available and encouraged people to use it. Many times we receive material that we feel likely has not really followed our standard operating procedures. So the worst-case scenario is someone opens a body-bag and sees hundreds of bone samples in there and will indiscriminately start sampling those and submitting them for expensive and laborious DNA tests. So ideally, this would be moderated by someone with a great deal of anthropological expertise that could determine the minimum number of people involved in this incident that they're reviewing, and sample DNA in a way that is most highly effective. That doesn't always occur. So we don't -- no, we don't always have control over what we do receive or how it's labelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, as far as the testing process is concerned, ultimately, in many instances, you find or declare a match, and we'll get into what is required in order to declare a match a little bit more precisely. But you heard, perhaps, in my summary my reference to your prior testimony distinguishing between the finding of a match and the closing of a case that is normally handled by a pathologist. I wonder if you could expanded on that a little bit so we understand what the difference is between those two things.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, with regard the DNA typing process, we operate a completely objective and blind system. So the samples come to us without any information where they came from, who they may be related to, and that applies both to the bone samples as well as the blood samples. They are immediately stripped of any such identifiers. So we then have an objective process of establishing a DNA profile and then doing computer matching. And we may have, let's say, a mother and two daughters have provided blood samples to help us try to identify that woman's missing son. We obtain a bone sample and generate a DNA profile and compare that to tens of thousands of family reference blood samples. We'll get a computerized score that says, There is similarity in some very interesting ways between the DNA profile from this bone sample and these donors relating to missing persons. And so we'll get a ranked list of possible associations. So lo and behold, this bone sample will have a high score, suggesting it may be maternally related to this woman. And then right below it, there'll be a high score suggesting that there may be a sibling relationship between one of the daughters, and likewise for the other sibling. Having then been alerted to this possible association by virtue of computational indices that I won't belabour further, we then take all the genetic information specifically for that missing person, in other words, we take, together, the mother's DNA profile and the two siblings' DNA profile and put it into a standard genetic kinship calculation with the genetic profile from the bone sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to ask you to slow down a little bit because you've got some very technical terms in there and I'm not sure how easy they are to interpret.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: So it is this final calculation that tells us the statistical strength with which this bone DNA profile can be considered to be related to the those family reference profiles in the way that this missing person has been stated to be related to those. In other words, what's the strength of the evidence that this bone sample came from the missing person for whom they provided a reference sample. And again, the system that we use can provide astronomical levels of support for that. Our minimum surety for issuing a DNA match report is 99.95 per cent sure. That means -- that can be translated into more every day terms, I suppose, by saying that there is one chance in 2.000 that this individual's DNA profile would have come from an unrelated individual instead of the person that we have issued the DNA match report on. But I want to go back and emphasise that that is our minimum threshold, one chance in 2.000 that this is an erroneous random match instead of the real match. Many times, instead of 99.95 per cent we would have 99., say, ten 9s or twelve 9s or something like that. So instead of one chance in 2.000, in a great majority of our cases it would be more on the order of one chance in a hundred billion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you, while we're on this topic, 65 ter 6273A. We'll need not to broadcast this document. 6723A. I don't believe we have a translation of this document, so I'm going to tell the Defence what it is. It is a case file relating to a body which was exhumed in connection with Bisina, a mass grave-site, and it relates to body number 40. You'll see at the top of the document an indication of BIS, Bisina, BIS, 01 SEK, which I believe is Sekovici. And then you'll see 040 B (f). And you'll see the name of the individual this relates to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, may I interject for just one moment. It occurs to me that in the discussion I've had so far with regard to the DNA match report, that I haven't yet answered your previous question regarding the difference between a DNA match report and case closure. If that's something you'd like me to do now, that would be fine. Or if you think it would be more useful to go through this, that would be fine as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I hadn't realised that, and I appreciate you pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you can explain it relatively briefly, we can do that. Or we can go through this first. So if you can explain it briefly, let's do that first.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I think that thematically it might make more sense to go ahead with that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: So I gave what may have been an unfortunately long-winded explanation of the DNA match report, but it is that match report that then is sent back to the submitting pathologist from whom we originally obtained the bone sample. Or today, we actually route that through the Bosnian national agency called the Missing Persons Institute, who now has authority for missing persons issues in Bosnia, and they provide that to the pathologist. But in effect, the result of the DNA test, in the form of a DNA match report, is sent back to the individual who has the remains. And as I just said, the strength of the identification is astronomically high on the DNA report but that person will then get the information on the missing person that the DNA match report says this is and ask, Is this consistent with the biologically determined age, sex, and stature of the remains? Is it consistent with what we know about the circumstances of this person's disappearance? In other words, was he recovered from a Srebrenica-related grave and had been registered as missing by the family members in association to the Srebrenica event? That type of circumstantial evidence. If there is any clothing, personal artifacts, or other characteristics of the case that the families could identify or would help them accept the identification, then the pathologist makes a determination, based on the scientific evidence from the DNA match report and all the other information that's available to him, that would allow him to exercise his legal authority to conclude an official identification and issue a death certificate. In the case of Srebrenica, in virtually all cases, this is done by Dr. Rifat Kesetovic at the Podrinje identification process [sic]. It's a facility that is a long-time partner of the ICMP. And that would -- that case closure then would also be the trigger for handing the identified body back to the family members and involve, indeed, their review of the case, will be present the to them. So that's difference between a DNA match report and case closure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that a DNA match report pays a part in the ultimate declaration of death, closure of a case, by the pathologist?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for the purposes -- for ICMP's purposes, identification purposes, you've indicated that the minimum threshold for surety in an identification is 99.95 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to show you is --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But we can't continue at this point in time. We must have our second break and then we will continue. We resume at quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, where we left off, I was asking you -- sorry. Where we left off, I was asking you how you know that this is a document that was sent off to the pathologist. And you were about to answer.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand I can use this pen to indicate things on the screen. I'll try that. But the reason I'm able to see immediately, it relates to these -- can you see my -- the cursor moving?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There we go. So it just seems easier to refer to this area that I'm outlining here. And here, this is a representation of the genetic profile of the individuals on this match report. And the way I can tell that this is one that we would be submitting externally to the pathologist in question is that these genetic types here are actually coded in a way that allows you to see how -- see what the relationships are amongst the individuals on this match report but not to actually know the genetic profile of the individual. And we do this for reasons of genetic privacy, genetic protection of the family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

Could you please encircle these two columns again. And if you could perhaps add a number 1 to the first one, number 2 to the second one, and indicate what is depicted in the two circles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I'm going to call them the coded genetic profile of the victim, that means the skeletonised remains; and, 2, the coded genetic profile - GP, genetic profile - of a family member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And there are additional ones below that I haven't circled that are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye tendered this, and it will be received, this marked document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1938, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just before we go to the next page, Dr. Parsons, you can see on this page at the bottom left-hand corner, a reference sample is indicated. And just for the sake of brevity, is that the sample -- a photograph of the sample that was tested in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's -- yes, that's the photo documentation of the bone sample in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that done in every case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just forever the record, the marked page is received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, briefly, can you tell us what we have here?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: This is a different version of the DNA report which is internal to the ICMP and contains uncoded genetic profiles. So the numerical entries in the cells there are those that would indicate to a geneticist what the real genetic profile of the individual is. As I mentioned before, we do not distribute that. Also, just distinguishing this sheet is a number of signature lines along the very bottom, and those reflect stages in a formal review process where, after the report is generated, it's then sent back to the DNA laboratory and all the data is, you know, examined de novo and then a signature indicates that it's correct. And the statistical calculations, for example, are also duplicated. So this is a form of redundant review that is typical of forensic reporting practices.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the statistical surety that's indicated of, statistical surety of relationship between the sample and the family members that's indicated in this report, could you just tell us or walk us through what that is as briefly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can blow up the section that follows the word "conclusion" near the bottom the page so that we can see it more clearly. Yeah, that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And hear it reads, for the benefit of the Defence because I don't think we have a translation of this. It says: "The DNA results obtained from the bone sample BIS 01 SEK 040 B (f) are 900e 15 times more likely if the bone sample originated from an individual related to the blood references in a manner as described on this report than if the bone sample originated from another unrelated individual in the general population. The probability of relatedness as described in this report is greater than 99.99999 per cent, when using prior odds of 1/7.000." First, can you tell us what the number "900e 15 times" actually means?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a notational shorthand for an exponential in base 10. So that means that 900 times 10 to the 15th. Which in turn means -- which, in turn, is a shorthand for adding an additional 15 zeros after the 900. And that number, translated into language, if I'm not mistaken, would be 900 trillion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the prior odds of 1 in 7.000, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And I would like to do that by referring back to that original 900 trillion number. It's not stated here, but I'll simply define it, that that number is the likelihood ratio. And the likelihood ratio is the result of the DNA test. And the -- within the formalities of forensic statistic, what a likelihood ratio is - please bear with me; it's a simple concept - is the factor by which one is more sure after having done a test than you were before. So there may have been some previous suspicion that this bone sample derives from this individual. Having done this DNA test, we're now 900 trillion times more sure than we were before. How sure we are in the end depends on how sure we were before we did the test. Because we know we're 900 trillion times more sure; how sure were we before? Well, that's where the prior odds come in; that's what that means. And in this case we considered that there was 1 chance in 7.000, before doing any DNA test, that this bone sample was this individual. And where we get that number is, at that time there was an estimate of 7.000 people missing from the Srebrenica event, we knew that this came from a Srebrenica-related grave, and so the prior odds, without doing a DNA test, that it's this particular named individual is only 1 in 7.000. When you update that uncertainty by 900 trillion times, you wind up being 99. a lot of nines after there. If you'll note, the report says its greater than 99. and then there are five 9s. Actually, there are more 9s in the real number; we don't bother to list them on our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, Dr. Parsons. And I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to actually tender the whole file, and it's 65 ter 06723A, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I take it this is -- I'm not sure about that because I have not an updated list, that it was on your last list; yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I apologise that you don't have an updated one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no reason for your apologies. That was perhaps a mistake in our office. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1939. And I understand this should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have one other document that I'd like to show Dr. Parsons and that's 65 ter 7191. This also should not be broadcast. Mr. President, because this is a spreadsheet with multiple tabs, we are going to have to display it through Sanction so that the witness can see it in e-court. Can we proceed with that, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, do you recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The sheet I'm looking at appears to be a title sheet that is not one that I'm familiar with, but it refers to -- ah, here we go. I'm sorry, I was looking at a different document. Yes, indeed. This is the cover sheet of an Excel file that the ICMP provided to your office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does it relate to the matching reports that were generated in the process you described through ICMP's DNA matching efforts?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if I could go to the first tab. Well, you can see a series of tabs here: One is entitled, "Srebrenica event"; another entitled, "Zepa event"; the third is, "cases inconclusively associated"; and there's a fourth tab indicating, "cases excluded as associated." Have you had a chance to review, generally, this file?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to the Srebrenica event, if we could just go to the first page of this, and maybe we can -- well, we can probably go through it. I just want to go briefly through the -- some of the captions here which you may be able to explain to the Trial Chamber. Let's pick the first entry here. Here we have a "date of birth" and then we have what's called "protocol ID." Can you tell us, basically, what a protocol ID is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, yes. So each of the horizontal entries relates to an individual DNA match report that has been listed. So, actually, the first column contains the name of the individual to whom the DNA match report relates. And then, more specifically, your question about the protocol ID, that is simply an internal ICMP tracking number that uniquely identifies the DNA match report in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we go to the next column, "case ID," can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's the -- the name of the sample, if you will. That's the coded information that is the identifier of the sample as it was received by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that the sample name that is given -- and we can see in the photograph of the other case file that I showed briefly, the one that indicated body 040 Bisina, Sekovici, is that the type of information that we see here?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yeah, without that match report, that's the number that would be listed in that column.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And here -- and then next to that, in column E, we have "ID ICMP." What's that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's another internal ICMP number that simply relates to the missing person. So the protocol ID is a unique identifier of the match report itself, and the ID ICMP number is the number that's associated with that reported missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, we can see after the ID ICMP we have a site name and we have "site co-ordinates," "jurisdiction," and then "date of submission." Can you tell us what the date of submission is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's the date upon which the ICMP issued to an external agent the DNA match report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Following that, we have the "date of disappearance" and the "place of disappearance." And from where does the ICMP obtain this office?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That information is obtained from family members who have reported the missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Following that we have, in the last column, the type of report. And here in the first entry we have a "main case," as distinguished from what we can see four lines down as a "re-association." Can you briefly outline the difference between the two for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: If there's a main case listed, that means that's -- that DNA match report is the first instance under which we have made an association between a bone sample and that missing person. In contrast to a re-association case where we have now found a second bone sample also relating to that same missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, we can see there's a tab for the Zepa event. Here on this page we can see certain items or certain individuals highlighted in a kind of a pinkish colour. Can you tell us what that means in the context of this chart?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yeah, this chart is the most recent of a series of such charts that we have provided to the -- to your office. And the ones that are highlighted on my screen - it's a bit beige compared to the grey - those are samples that are new, you know, the match reports that are new since the last time we had presented a list to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to just draw your attention to the last two tabs which are "cases inconclusively associated" and "cases excluded respectively." Now, with respect to the cases that are inconclusively associated, can you tell us what that generally means?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, yes. A little bit of background here, if I may. These lists relating to match reports for Srebrenica have been brought together at the request of the ICTY. These are not normally -- this is not a product of the ICMP accredited forensic programme, in other words, we don't generally make these lists ourselves. So in the past we have provided, as I mentioned before, a number of lists to you. As time has gone by, we've obtained additional information about some of these cases that were previously -- that were listed on previous lists. And in this instance we've made some -- a number of corrections to the previous list or categorised some cases differently to increase the clarity of what's going on here. So the predominant means by which a match report and an individual's name will be included on any of these lists is that the family has reported that individual as missing as a result of the fall of Srebrenica in July of 1995. And that was the criteria under which we assembled this list to provide to you. As a result of additional information and/or additional investigation, this most recent list that we've provided to you contains these additional categories that -- that we hope to clarify. In describing those, it actually might be easiest, if you don't mind, if we could refer to the tab that says, "cases excluded as associated."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We can do that.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: And if we could tab over to the right, where we have the "ICMP comment." So what we have here, on this entire tab, is six cases that the ICMP no longer considers to be related to the Srebrenica event and a brief comment that indicates why that -- why we believe that now, in contrast to having included it before. The explanations for those get a little bit complicated. I mean, they're clear to me, but it requires a bit of discussion about it. But to give you an idea of the types of things that come into play, I think it's necessary for me to talk a little bit about one as an example. So let's look at the very first one listed here, where the ICMP comment is, "two brothers missing," and by that we mean reported missing to us, "one reported missing from July 1995, the other from 1992. The one from 1995 has been identified on a Cancari case." That means a case coming from a grave known to be associated with Srebrenica. And therefore this one should be from the other brother who wasn't reported missing from 1995 but from 1992. Underlying this, a point that will help in the understanding is that DNA, under many circumstances depending on the reference samples involved, cannot distinguish between siblings. So if you have only the parents or one parent and some siblings as references, you can't -- if there are multiple other siblings missing, the DNA, based on those references, won't be able to distinguish which sibling is which. So the DNA match report is actually issued in two names. We have two siblings reported missing to us. The DNA doesn't tell us which is which. And so we've put both of their names on the match report. We know it's one of them; we can't tell which it is. In this case, we've actually -- we've had two brothers reported missing. Both names are on both match reports, but one of them comes from a grave known to be associated with Srebrenica. So by a process of elimination, we've now cleaned a list and pulled that one off because the second sibling is not associated with -- was not reported as associated with Srebrenica so he's been removed from the list. I would be happy to clarify that more, if there's any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put a question to the witness in relation to, I think it was column E. Perhaps we can go back there. The ID ICMP column. And further to the left, please. Yes. No, I think we need another page. Perhaps the first one that was ... Yes, thank you. We see the name listed three times in the line 5, 6, 7. I don't want to read out the name. We have identical ID ICMP numbers in column E but different entries in the case ID. I would like to invite you to explain that for me so that I have a better understanding of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my pleasure. What we can't see on the screen right now, and we would see if we went over to the right, is -- okay. Here we go. Except I can't ... Can someone remind me, please, which of the rows we're talking about? You said it was 4, 5, and 6?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it was 5, 6, 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, let's say -- it looks to me like 6, 7, and 8, all in the name of a single individual with a single ID ICMP; agreed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 5, 6, 7. We can't count. But I'm referring to a specific number, and this is identical in three columns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the screen that I'm looking at, these are rows listed as 6, 7 and 8. On the one I'm looking at. But I think we're talking exactly about the same thing. So let's scroll to the right briefly; we don't need to overdo this. But, indeed, with regard to the type of report, we have, for these three different listings all relating to the same named individual, we have a main case and two re-associations. So now let's go back to the left where we can all -- where we can visualize everything. So these three match reports relate to three different samples that were submitted for DNA testing to the ICMP. In the one that's listed as the main case, that was the first sample that was seen to match to the family members of this particular missing person who is designated by ID ICMP as number 3175. Two of the other samples were submitted independently and then also were different body parts of the same individual. So we have three different body parts that have been sampled for DNA, all of which derive from the same individual and therefore have the same ICMP ID number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But found in different graves; is that correct? I see the one column to the right, Cancari, Kamenica, and Cancari, Zvornik it should read, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think that these were not from separate graves. I don't have definitive information, but the reason I say that is because of the case ID number just there on the screen. They all relate -- they all come from CR-05. And by convention, that would be the Cancari Road grave number 5. So I can see how there's a little confusion about the site name. Actually, both Cancari and Kamenica are alternate names, really, for the same place, and so this would be an instance of when the information was recorded on the sample submissions sheet in one instance somebody wrote Cancari in the other instance they wrote Kamenica. But by looking at the sample codes there, the case ID, it looks to me very much like those are all three from the Cancari Road 5 grave. And they would be different fragments of the same individual that recovered -- not able to be associated with each other by traditional means but were all recovered from that secondary, co-mingled, and fragmented grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you might also notice that the site co-ordinates for the entries that are listed are identical for all three entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the situation in the entries. This document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1940, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that we will submit this under -- on a CD, and it should be under seal as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Under seal, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, now it's your turn to commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Hello to the witness. And regardless of the fact that we are close to the end of the day, I hope that the proceedings will end with God's will and not as I wish. I wish you a pleasant stay here and my greetings to you on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question relates to part of your report, and it's this: When Mr. Vanderpuye, on page 48, provided information about you, he said that you were director of forensic science International Commission of Missing Persons. Is it a forensic science centre? And why is it called a forensic science centre if you're unrelated to any court?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, it's not a forensic science centre, nor is it called a forensic science centre. I am the director of a division within the ICMP that is called the forensic sciences division, and so I have oversight over the conduct of forensic science as conducted by the ICMP. We conduct scientific investigations according to the norms of forensic science and therefore that's what our division is called. Furthermore, as we can see in today's proceedings, the results of our findings are very much related to legal processes, and it seems entirely reasonable to me to apply the word "forensic." Moreover, we are accredited as a forensic institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why, then, there is no department that would be connected to and responsible for certain information as in this case when you are working for the International Tribunal? Why do you not have somebody who's going to be responsible to this Court if you are presenting us with this information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't know if it's a translation issue, but I don't really understand your question. Responsible for certain information? I'm responsible for the testimony I'm giving here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask my question again. If you have a team that works in Bosnia for the purposes of this Tribunal and you said that they were located in Tuzla or in Sarajevo, then how is it that you did not assign a certain person who would be responsible to this International Tribunal for work that it does for the Tribunal, if the whole organisation, as such, is not answerable to the Court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The work that the ICMP conducts is not for the purposes of this Tribunal. We do not do work for the Tribunal. We identify individuals to turn them back to their family members, to turn the family members -- to turn the loved ones back to the family members, and to assist the government in Bosnia for taking responsibility for the multifaceted issues associated with missing persons. In the conduct of our work, it has become apparent to this Court that the results of our work have some relevance, it seems. And it is in that capacity that we have shared our information and it brings me here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you here because you wanted to be here, are you here because it's your own decision, or were you invited here by an organ that is related to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We have been asked to provide information by the Office of the Prosecutor in support of the Tribunal and we agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you were engaged by the Tribunal. Then why is there no person who is responsible to this Tribunal for what it does and for the reports that it submits? That's what I'm asking you. Why do you not want to be held responsible for what you're reporting on and for your own work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Your allegations, the basis of your question, doesn't have any standing. I'm responsible for what I report here. Why would you say we're not responsible? I don't understand what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could court proceedings be initiated against you for the findings that you get by matching samples with DNA and the results that you submit to the Court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 42 of today's transcript, I believe it was line 5, Mr. Vanderpuye, the Prosecutor, asked you who supervises the work of the commission. Could you tell the Court who monitors the reports that the commission produces and which are submitted to courts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, the commission itself is made up of a number of commissioners that take responsibility for the conduct and existence of the ICMP. With regard to monitoring of the forensic quality of our reports, I would refer again to some of the quality control initiatives that have been previously covered, particularly with regard to our international accreditation of our scientific processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, for the work that you do, are you responsible to your employer, to the commission, or to the institution for which you are working? Thank you. To who are you responsible judicially, in terms of judicial sanctions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I'm responsible to my employer, the International Commission on Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to state for the record that on page 42 of today's transcript, other than you just put on the record, Mr. Vanderpuye didn't ask anything because he was at that point reading the summary. This is a difference. And the summary is not in evidence. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You are right. Based on what Mr. Vanderpuye said, I asked my question regarding the monitoring of the work, whether it was the employer or the organ commissioning the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: To whom are you responsible after you complete your work? Is it the body that financed you, your employer, or whoever it was that commissioned you to do the work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what part of our work you're referring to. The work that is conducted at grave-sites is done so under court order of the Bosnian State Court. And the recipients of our DNA match reports, I have been -- are court appointed -- state appointed pathologists who are authorised to submit samples to us and to whom we release reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will give an example. On page 47, I believe it was line 10, you said that you were engaged because of the tsunami that occurred and during Hurricane Katarina. My question is this: Who engaged you to search for missing persons there and do your findings match the causes for why these people went missing? And I apologise, in your findings, did you describe the causes why a certain person went missing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: You've asked about our engagement in the tsunami and I'll begin with that. As a result of the tsunami in 2006, I believe it was, there was a large international effort to respond to this horrific natural catastrophe that affected the citizens of multiple countries. So forensic teams from many nations were deployed on site, in this case to Thailand, which was undertaking a major response to recover and identify the people -- the thousands of people that were killed there. And under the authority of the Thai national police, whose actual jurisdiction this was, multinational forensic teams became involved to pull together to try to make the recoveries and the identifications. As a result of this major international effort, the ICMP was invited to assist based on our expertise with regard to this kind of difficult samples, and we generated victim profiles and provided DNA match reports in a very, very similar manner to that I've described here. We did not make any statements or conclusions relating to cause of death. In the case of Hurricane Katarina, the responsible authority that requested our assistance --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The first example was sufficient, just because of time. Since you've now determined the cause of the disaster, you say it was a natural disaster, were you sure that it was a natural disaster, or was it some other disaster caused by a human factor, since there is no return wave in a tsunami? There is a strike wave in case of tsunamis, and there was a return wave there. So how did you conclude that it was a natural disaster?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP does not have an opinion on whether a tsunami was a natural disaster or not. I leave that for a more general expertise. I think most people in the world consider a tidal wave to be a natural disaster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At least it was an occurrence in the nature. We have to adjourn for today. We are at the end of today's hearing. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in this courtroom. Sir, I have to remind you that it is not allowed to have contact with either party during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I wish you a good stay. And we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of February, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
